article.title: The Day After
article.author: Mike Guynn
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On November 3, 2026, Los Angeles voters will decide who leads their city. But on November 4, 2026 the rent will still be due. Homelessness, housing affordability, public safety, neighborhood services, and public trust will remain urgent concerns. The election will change the leadership question, not eliminate the challenges. The real test is not simply whether Karen Bass wins reelection or Nithya Raman becomes mayor. It is whether residents can turn their expectations into measurable commitments and ensure that whoever occupies City Hall answers to the people. If Raman Wins, the Scrutiny Begins A new mayor would inherit a city confronting difficult questions about housing, homelessness, public safety, infrastructure, and government transparency. A change in leadership might create an opportunity for different approaches, but it would not guarantee better outcomes. Related: Nithya Raman, Karen Bass and the Politics of Accountability in Los Angeles If Raman wins, residents should demand a public 100-day action plan identifying the administration’s priorities, responsible departments, funding sources, deadlines, and measures of success. Homelessness initiatives should be evaluated through housing placements, long-term stability, available services, and transparent spending. Housing policies should be assessed by completed homes, affordability, and access for working families. Public safety commitments should include meaningful reporting on emergency response, staffing, and community concerns. The standard must be evidence, not enthusiasm. A new administration deserves an opportunity to govern, but it does not deserve a blank check. If Bass Wins, Reelection Must Mean Results If Bass wins another term, her victory should represent renewed responsibility, not an exemption from criticism. Supporters may point to her administration’s efforts on homelessness, housing, and public safety. Critics may question the pace of progress, policy effectiveness, or responses to major crises. These competing assessments should be examined against documented outcomes, independent evaluations, and residents’ experiences. A second Bass administration should face the same demand for a public 100-day plan, transparent spending, and regular progress reports. Residents affected by the Palisades fire and other emergencies deserve clear information about recovery, rebuilding obstacles, and promised assistance. Reelection does not close the public record on a first term. It opens another chapter in which the administration must explain what worked, what failed, and what comes next. Build an Accountability Movement Regardless of the winner, Los Angeles needs a permanent, nonpartisan civic accountability network. Neighborhood councils, tenant associations, business owners, community organizations, labor groups, and residents should establish measurable priorities, monitor city budgets, examine public contracts, attend hearings, and publish quarterly progress reports grounded in verifiable information. The objective is not to manufacture scandals or attack politicians personally. It is to make government performance visible and public commitments difficult to forget. Officials should answer specific questions. When deadlines are missed, they should explain why. When programs succeed, the public should acknowledge progress. When spending changes, residents deserve to understand the trade-offs. Participation must extend to every neighborhood, including communities too often overlooked. Meetings, reports, and opportunities to participate should accommodate different languages, disabilities, and working schedules. Accountability cannot belong exclusively to those with political connections or abundant free time. Follow the Money Every major promise eventually meets a budget. Residents deserve to know what initiatives cost, where funding comes from, which services compete for those dollars, and whether the results justify the investment. Transparency is not an accusation of wrongdoing. It is a basic requirement of responsible government. Los Angeles should not have to choose between compassion and competence, or between public safety and civil rights. Residents deserve policies that are effective, financially responsible, and open to scrutiny. November 5: The Public Takes Its Seat The day after the election, residents should begin organizing—not waiting for the next campaign, the next crisis, or the next broken promise. Invite neighbors. Set priorities. Establish measurable goals. Track spending. Attend public meetings. Publish findings. Return for answers. Keep the effort peaceful, lawful, and independent of any single politician or party. If Raman wins, hold her accountable. If Bass wins, hold her accountable. Recognize genuine progress, document shortcomings, and demand corrective action. The ballot determines who occupies City Hall. It does not surrender the people’s power to question, challenge, and demand results. On November 5, 2026 Los Angeles must ask more than who won. What was promised? What will be delivered? Who will measure the results? When will the public return to demand answers? The mayor may lead the city. The people must hold the government accountable. The election ends. Accountability begins. “THE VILLAGE SAGE” This article was produced by Micheal's Substack .
